opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that a Foundation Agent is one model that can generalize along two axes at the same time. The first axis is the number of skills it can do, and the second is the number of embodiments it can control, meaning the different bodies it can inhabit and the different realities it can operate in.

If you look at what my team has done over the past few years, a lot of it has been probing those axes one at a time. In Minecraft, with projects like MineDojo and Voyager, we explored an agent that keeps learning new skills open-endedly in a very rich virtual world. With work like Eureka, we looked at using language models to write reward functions so robots can learn really dexterous skills, like pen spinning, in simulation and then transfer that to the real world. And with MetaMorph, we trained a single policy that can control many different robot body shapes. Each of those is one slice of the bigger picture.

The key insight that ties it together is that, to a model, the physical world is just another reality. If you can train an agent across ten thousand different simulated worlds, each with different physics, different visuals, and different bodies, then the real world becomes the ten-thousand-and-first simulation. If the agent can handle that whole distribution, it should generalize to reality without ever being specifically tuned for it. So simulation at massive scale, running orders of magnitude faster than real time on GPUs, is how we get the data diversity we need. Real robot data is expensive and slow, and there's no internet-scale dataset of motor control the way there is for text.

On the interface side, I think of it as embodiment as a prompt. You can describe the body and the action space to the model, the same way you prompt an LLM with a task, and the same underlying model figures out how to act. Whether the output is keyboard and mouse actions in a game, joint torques for a humanoid, or movements for a robot arm, it's a different decoding of the same core understanding of the world: physics, causality, goals, and planning.

So the end state I'm excited about is one model, many bodies, many worlds. It plays a video game, runs a character in a virtual world, and drives a humanoid robot in your kitchen, all from the same set of weights. We're not there yet, but I think it's a very clear north star, and the pieces are starting to come together: large multimodal models, scalable simulation, and better robot hardware all arriving at the same time.

r001.rationale: It describes “one model” that can act through game controls and robot bodies, including a humanoid robot.

r002.rationale: It explicitly names the number of skills the model can perform as its first axis.

r003.rationale: It explicitly names the number of embodiments, or bodies the model can control, as its second axis.

r004.rationale: It describes training across simulated worlds and generalizing to reality, but names only skills and embodiments as the Foundation Agent’s axes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, the Foundation Agent is really one model that takes in an embodiment, takes in a world, takes in a set of instructions, and produces actions. And the key insight is that if you squint, a virtual agent and a physical agent aren't that different. Whether it's Minecraft or a humanoid robot, you've got some observation stream, usually pixels, you've got some action space, and you've got a task specified in language. The surface form differs, but the underlying problem is the same: perceive, reason, act, repeat.

So the bet is that we can train across all of these embodiments at once. We did this with MineDojo and Voyager on the virtual side, and then with things like Eureka and GR00T on the physical side, and what you start to see is that skills transfer. A model that learns long-horizon planning in a game is learning something that's useful for a robot stacking dishes. The game is just a very cheap, very scalable simulator.

The axis I care most about is actually three things: generalizing across skills, generalizing across embodiments, and generalizing across realities, meaning from simulation to the real world. If you can scale along all three, then the physical world is just one more reality the agent has visited. And simulation gives us essentially unlimited data in a way the physical world never will, so we front-load the learning there and then close the gap with a relatively small amount of real-world data.

The analogy I like is that GPT didn't need a separate model for poetry and code and legal documents. Language was the unifying interface. For agents, I think action is the unifying interface, and the embodiment is just a prompt. You tell the model what body it's wearing today, and it figures out the rest. That's the dream, anyway. We're clearly not there yet, but every year the gap between the virtual and physical side gets smaller.

r001.rationale: It describes a single model that takes an embodiment and world as input and produces actions, covering virtual and physical agents.

r002.rationale: It explicitly names generalizing across skills as one of the three axes.

r003.rationale: It explicitly names generalizing across embodiments as an axis and describes the embodiment as the body the agent wears.

r004.rationale: It explicitly names generalizing across realities, including the transition from simulation to the real world.

astra-6.text:
I think of a Foundation Agent as a model that can act across many different worlds and embodiments. A language model can handle many tasks through a common interface—text. For an agent, the question is: can we build a similarly general interface for observations, actions, and goals, whether you’re controlling a video game character, a simulated robot, or a physical robot?

You don’t want to learn everything from scratch for each body. Planning, understanding objects, and reasoning about what happens when you take an action should be transferable. But the way you execute that action depends on your embodiment. A humanoid and a robot arm might understand the same goal, but they have very different ways of accomplishing it.

My vision is to use virtual worlds as a rich training ground, where agents can encounter diverse tasks and learn through interaction at scale. Then physical experience helps ground those capabilities in the real world, with its uncertainty and constraints. Simulation won’t magically solve transfer. The challenge is learning what’s shared across worlds while adapting to what’s different. That’s the kind of generalization I’d want a Foundation Agent to achieve.

r001.rationale: Describes one model acting across virtual worlds and physical embodiments, including game characters, simulated robots, and physical robots.

r002.rationale: Says planning, object understanding, and reasoning about action outcomes should transfer across tasks.

r003.rationale: Explicitly discusses different embodiments, contrasting a humanoid with a robot arm and their different ways of acting.

r004.rationale: Frames the vision around acting across many worlds, using virtual worlds for training and grounding capabilities in the real world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of a Foundation Agent as a single model that can act across many different environments and embodiments. A language model takes in tokens and predicts the next token. An agent needs to take in observations, understand a goal, and produce actions—and ideally, those capabilities should transfer across a video game, a simulated robot, and a physical robot.

The key is to share the knowledge while adapting how it gets expressed. Planning how to navigate around an obstacle is useful across many bodies, but pressing a keyboard key is very different from commanding a robot’s joints. So you want a shared core for perception, reasoning, and planning, with interfaces that translate observations and actions for each embodiment.

Virtual worlds are a powerful training ground because you can generate diverse tasks and collect experience at scale. But simulation alone isn’t enough. Physical systems introduce uncertainty, contact, latency, and consequences that a simulator may miss. You need real-world experience to ground those capabilities.

The exciting possibility is that learning becomes cumulative: experience in one environment helps the agent learn another more efficiently, rather than requiring us to train a new specialist from scratch every time.

r001.rationale: It describes a single model acting across a video game, a simulated robot, and a physical robot.

r002.rationale: It names perception, reasoning, and planning, but does not clearly identify generalization across skills as an axis of the vision.

r003.rationale: It explicitly discusses transferring capabilities across different bodies and adapting interfaces for each embodiment.

r004.rationale: It describes transfer across environments, including virtual worlds and the physical real world.
